Senate
AK-Sen
Both parties appear to be maneuvering to ensure that their preferred minor candidates make it to the November general election in Alaska’s Senate race alongside the two frontrunners, Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola, according to FEC filings first flagged by CNN’s Patrick Svitek (https://x.com/PatrickSvitek/status/2083261775760298074) .
A super PAC formed just days ago called Fair Deal Alaska has already reported spending almost $420,000 (https://www.fec.gov/data/independent-expenditures/?data_type=efiling&committee_id=C00957555&is_notice=true&most_recent=true) on mailers, ads, and phone calls, a small portion of which is devoted to attacking Peltola. But the lion’s share is intended to boost two perennial candidates: Democrat Carol Hafner and Green Party member Richard Grayson.
Meanwhile, a different super PAC, Right for Alaska, has spent $515,000 (https://www.fec.gov/data/independent-expenditures/?data_type=processed&most_recent=true&q_spender=C00944611&is_notice=true) on ads in the same contest. One half of that expenditure is getting used to go after Sullivan while the other is aimed at elevating Republican Jerry Heikes, another serial candidate, and Skip Southworth, a member of the Alaskan Party. That party is a successor to the far-right Alaska Independence Party, which dissolved last year (https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/01/13/alaskas-third-largest-political-party-votes-to-dissolve-raising-uncertainty-for-its-19000-members/) but was reconstituted (https://mustreadalaska.com/alaskan-party-officially-recognized-as-political-group-by-alaska-division-of-elections-former-aip-leaders-urge-re-registration/) under a new name earlier this year.
The reason for these dueling efforts is Alaska’s unique primary that’s coming up on Aug. 18. All 16 candidates from all parties will run together on a single ballot, with the top four vote-getters advancing to the general election.
That fall contest will be decided by ranked-choice voting, so Republicans would almost certainly prefer that the third and fourth options lean to the left in the hopes that some voters will cast ballots for them while failing to rank Peltola. Democrats, meanwhile, would want the exact opposite.
Governors
KS-Gov
The Democratic primary in the race to succeed term-limited Kansas Gov. Laura Kelly has grown negative ahead of Tuesday’s election as the leading contenders clash over data centers and a stadium deal for the NFL’s Kansas City Chiefs.
Kelly’s preferred successor, state Sen. Ethan Corson, has dominated the field financially, according to new fundraising reports (https://www.salina.com/story/news/politics/government/2026/07/31/corson-builds-fundraising-lead-in-democratic-race-for-kansas-governor/91079382007/) , but has faced sharp attacks from a fellow state senator, Cindy Holscher.

Leading Off
CA Ballot
California voters will decide this fall (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316600442.html) whether to overhaul the state’s rules for recall elections—rules that helped end one governor’s career while potentially saving another’s.
In any recall election against state-level officials, including the governor and members of the legislature, ballots currently consist of two separate questions (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) .
Voters are first asked a “yes” or “no” question about whether they want to remove the incumbent. They’re then asked to pick among the candidates vying to replace them—a contest that the incumbent cannot run in. These results, though, only matter if a majority votes “yes” on the first question.
If “yes” prevails, however, the successor could get elected with much less than a majority of the vote. That’s because all the candidates from all parties run on a single ballot without any primary or runoff to winnow the field.
But Proposition 5, which the state’s Democratic-led legislature voted to place on this year’s ballot back in 2024 (https://news.ballotpedia.org/2024/09/03/california-voters-will-decide-on-amendment-to-eliminate-successor-election-at-state-officer-recall-elections-in-2026/) , would amend the state constitution to change this process.
Under the proposed amendment, voters would simply be asked (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/news-releases-and-advisories/2026-news-releases-and-advisories/secretary-state-shirley-n-weber-phd-assigns-numbers-november-ballot-measures-invites-ballot-arguments) whether or not they want to recall the incumbent. If the governor is ousted, the lieutenant governor would automatically take over. Other offices, according to the proposed amendment (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/sca-1-24.pdf#page=3) , would be “filled in accordance with this Constitution and statute.”
If the governor is removed, what happens next would depend on the political calendar.
If the removal were to happen during the first two years of a governor’s term and ahead of the filing deadline for the next statewide primary, an election for their permanent replacement would take place alongside that primary.
All candidates would compete on a single ballot as they do now, but under the new rules, a majority would be necessary to win outright. If no one were to clear that threshold, the top-two vote-getters, regardless of party, would advance to a runoff coinciding with the November general election. In addition, the ousted governor would be eligible to compete in this contest.
If a recall were to take place outside this period, though, the lieutenant governor would serve as governor for the remainder of the term.
Two governors, both Democrats, have faced recall elections during the 21st century, but their fates diverged.
In 2003, Republicans targeted Gov. Gray Davis, who had won a second term the previous year, as the state’s ongoing energy crisis (https://www.cnn.com/2003/ALLPOLITICS/10/06/energy.crisis/index.html) left him unpopular. GOP Rep. Darrell Issa, one of the wealthiest members of Congress, bankrolled the recall campaign (https://www.the-downballot.com/p/morning-digest-after-saying-hes-not) with the intention of running to replace the incumbent.
A far-better known Republican, though, took advantage of Issa’s efforts. Arnold Schwarzenegger, the “Terminator” star who had spent decades at the top of Hollywood’s A-list, announced his campaign (https://www.cnn.com/2003/ALLPOLITICS/08/06/candidates.announce/) on “The Tonight Show” and instantly gobbled up all the attention. Issa, who no longer saw a path to victory, tearfully announced (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=T2tdOqCwqww) he would stay out of the race.
The GOP, though, wasn’t Davis’ only problem. Lt. Gov. Cruz Bustamante, a fellow Democrat, initially said (https://www.kqed.org/news/11870960/should-a-democrat-run-in-the-newsom-recall-we-asked-cruz-bustamante) he would “absolutely, 100%” not run as a replacement candidate, but he soon went back on that pledge and became one of the 135 people who placed their name on the ballot (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_California_gubernatorial_recall_election#/media/File:Sample_ballot_for_CA_recall.png) .
The lieutenant governor and his allies tried to thread the needle by pushing the slogan “No on recall, Yes on Bustamante.” However, they struggled to sell that awkward pitch even before Bustamante started criticizing the incumbent (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-sep-02-me-analysis2-story.html) in the evident hope that the recall would succeed and Bustamante would become his successor.
A 55-45 majority (https://uselectionatlas.org/RESULTS/state.php?fips=6&year=2003&f=0&off=5&elect=0) voted to remove Davis from office, but Californians didn’t want Bustamante as their new governor. Schwarzenegger instead prevailed over the massive field with 49% of the vote as Bustamante finished a distant second with 31%.
Gov. Gavin Newsom and his allies were determined to avoid a repeat of that debacle 18 years later when Republicans, who used the governor’s attendance at a high-end party (https://www.politico.com/states/california/story/2020/11/13/newsom-faces-backlash-after-attending-french-laundry-dinner-party-1336419) during the COVID pandemic as a pretext, placed a recall on the 2021 ballot.
Newsom’s side successfully discouraged (https://www.dailykos.com/stories/2021/3/1/2018561/elections/Morning-Digest-Top-New-York-Democrats-start-calling-for-Cuomo-to-be-primaried-but-who-will-run/#6) prominent Democrats from running as backup candidates and framed the race as a choice between the governor and far-right extremists.
Newsom’s argument became even easier when conservative radio host Larry Elder blew past (https://www.dailykos.com/stories/2021/9/15/2052274/elections/Morning-Digest-California-Gov-Gavin-Newsom-defeats-recall-vote-in-a-landslide/) more mainstream Republicans like former San Diego Mayor Kevin Faulconer when pollsters asked voters whom they favored on the second question.
Elder ultimately scored 48% (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/complete-sov.pdf#page=13) of the vote, while a little-known Democrat took a distant second with just 10%. But unlike in Schwarzenegger’s contest, the question proved to be meaningless. Voters rejected the recall 62-38, and Newsom went on to handily secure a second term the following year.

Dan Sullivan and former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola, according to FEC filings first flagged by CNN’s Patrick Svitek (https://x.com/PatrickSvitek/status/2083261775760298074) .
A super PAC formed just days ago called Fair Deal Alaska has already reported spending almost $420,000 (https://www.fec.gov/data/independent-expenditures/?data_type=efiling&committee_id=C00957555&is_notice=true&most_recent=true) on mailers, ads, and phone calls, a small portion of which is devoted to attacking Peltola. One half of that expenditure is getting used to go after Sullivan while the other is aimed at elevating Republican Jerry Heikes, another serial candidate, and Skip Southworth, a member of the Alaskan Party. That fall contest will be decided by ranked-choice voting, so Republicans would almost certainly prefer that the third and fourth options lean to the left in the hopes that some voters will cast ballots for them while failing to rank Peltola. Democrats, meanwhile, would want the exact opposite.

Senate Constitutional Amendment
No. 1
CHAPTER 204
A resolution to propose to the people of the State of California an amendment to the Constitution of the State, by amending Sections 15 and 17 of Article II thereof, and by amending Section 10 of Article V thereof, relating to elections.
[
Filed with
Secretary of State
September 10, 2024.
]
LEGISLATIVE COUNSEL'S DIGEST
SCA 1, Newman.
Elections: recall of state officers.
The California Constitution provides that voters may recall a state officer by majority vote and, in the same election, elect a successor with a plurality of the vote. The Constitution prohibits an officer who is the subject of a recall election from being a candidate for successor.
The Constitution provides that the Lieutenant Governor becomes Governor when a vacancy occurs in the office of Governor, and requires the Lieutenant Governor to act as Governor during the impeachment, absence from the state, or other temporary disability of the Governor or of a Governor-elect who fails to take office. When a recall of the Governor is initiated, the Constitution requires the Lieutenant Governor to perform the recall duties of the Governor. The Constitution requires the Governor to fill vacancies in certain judicial and executive offices by
appointment, as specified.
This measure would eliminate the successor election for a recalled state officer and instead provide, in the event an officer is removed in a recall election, that the office will remain vacant until it is filled in accordance with the Constitution and statute. The measure would repeal the prohibition against the officer subject to the recall being a candidate to fill the office in a special election, but would prohibit the appointment of the officer subject to the recall election to fill the vacancy.
If the Governor is removed from office in a recall election, this measure would provide that the Lieutenant Governor will become Governor for the remainder of the unexpired term. If the Governor is removed from office by recall before the close of the nomination period for the next statewide election during the first two years of the Governor’s term, the measure would provide for a special election
to be held to replace the Governor for the remainder of the unexpired term, to be consolidated with the next statewide primary election and, if necessary, the subsequent statewide general election. The measure would require the Secretary of State to perform the recall duties of the Governor when a recall of the Governor is initiated. The measure would require the Controller to perform the recall duties of the Governor and Secretary of State if recalls of those two officers are initiated at the same time.
If adopted by the Legislature, the measure would appear on the ballot at the November 3, 2026, statewide general election.

Vote:
2/3
Appropriation:
NO
Fiscal Committee:
YES
Local Program:
NO
Bill Text
Resolved by the Senate, the Assembly concurring, That the Legislature of the State of California at its 2023–24 Regular Session commencing on the fifth day of December 2022, two-thirds of the membership of each house concurring, hereby proposes to the people of the State of California that the Constitution of the State be amended as follows:
First—
That Section 15 of Article II thereof is amended to read:
SEC. 15.
(a) An election to determine whether to recall an officer shall be called by the Governor and held not less than 60 days nor more than 80 days from the date of certification of sufficient signatures.
(b) A recall election may be conducted within 180 days from the date of certification of sufficient signatures in order that the election may be consolidated with the next regularly scheduled election occurring wholly or partially within the same jurisdiction in which the recall election is held, if the number of voters eligible to vote at that next regularly scheduled election equal at least 50
percent of all the voters eligible to vote at the recall election.
(c) If the majority vote on the question is to recall, the officer is removed and the office shall be vacant. The vacancy shall be filled in accordance with this Constitution and statute, provided that the officer who was the subject of the recall election shall not be appointed to fill the vacancy in that office.
Second—
That Section 17 of Article II thereof is amended to read:
SEC. 17.
If recall of the Governor or Secretary of State is initiated, the recall duties of that office shall be performed by the Secretary of State or Controller, respectively. If recalls of the Governor and Secretary of State are initiated at the same time, the recall duties of both offices shall be performed by the Controller.
Third—
That Section 10 of Article V thereof is amended to read:
SEC. 10.
(a) The Lieutenant Governor shall become Governor when a vacancy occurs in the office of Governor.
(b) Notwithstanding subdivision (c) of Section 15 of Article II, if the Governor is removed from office by recall, the Lieutenant Governor shall become Governor for the remainder of the unexpired term. If the Governor is removed from office by recall before the close of the nomination period for the next statewide election during the first two years of the Governor’s term, a special election shall be called to replace the Governor and shall be consolidated with the statewide primary election and, if necessary, the subsequent statewide general
election. If a candidate receives a majority of the votes in the special election that is consolidated with the statewide primary election, that candidate shall become Governor for the remainder of the unexpired term. If no candidate receives a majority of the votes, the top two vote-getters shall compete in a special election consolidated with the subsequent statewide general election, and the winner of that election shall become Governor for the remainder of the unexpired term.
(c) The Lieutenant Governor shall act as Governor during the impeachment, absence from the State, or other temporary disability of the Governor or of a Governor-elect who fails to take office.
(d) The Legislature shall provide an order of precedence after the Lieutenant Governor for succession to the
office of Governor and for the temporary exercise of the Governor’s functions.
(e) The Supreme Court has exclusive jurisdiction to determine all questions arising under this section.
(f) Standing to raise questions of vacancy or temporary disability is vested exclusively in a body provided by statute.
Fourth—
This measure shall appear on the ballot at the November 3, 2026, statewide general election.

##### Recall Reform (2026)
California’s recall election process was designed as a democratic safeguard to hold corrupt or abusive officials accountable.
However, under current law, the recall ballot presents voters with two connected questions: **(1)** Should the official be recalled? and **(2)** If so, who should replace them?
These two questions together create a dangerous loophole.
An elected official can be removed by a narrow majority.
Then, a candidate listed in question #2 can win the office with far less than 50% of the votes cast in the election.
This encourages political actors to target officials they couldn’t defeat in a regular election and to install replacements who lack broad public support.
We saw this dynamic play out during the 2021 gubernatorial recall attempt.
Although voters overwhelmingly rejected the recall by nearly the exact margin as the original gubernatorial election, California taxpayers were forced to pay over **$200 million** for an unnecessary election.
Nearly 70% of California likely voters called the effort a waste of taxpayer money.
Had the recall succeeded, the leading replacement candidate would have taken office with only about 28% support from recall voters.
Proposition 5 enacts a single, commonsense fix to restore fairness and integrity: **it removes the second question from state recall ballots.**

When a state legislator or a statewide official such as the governor faces a recall, voters are asked two questions: Should the lawmaker or official be removed from office?
And who should replace them?
Proposition 5 would eliminate the successor question.
If a statewide officeholder is recalled, the governor would appoint a replacement, while legislative vacancies would be filled by special election.
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would serve until another governor is elected.

California’s current recall system allows a replacement candidate to take office without winning the support of a majority of voters.
In the unsuccessful 2021 recall of Gov.

Getting rid of the replacement question keeps the recall election focused on the official facing removal.

Voters who recall a governor, attorney general or secretary of state should not have to wait months to pick a replacement — all while the position is filled by someone who was not elected to the job.

An elected official can be removed by a narrow majority.
Then, a candidate listed in question #2 can win the office with far less than 50% of the votes cast in the election.
This encourages political actors to target officials they couldn’t defeat in a regular election and to install replacements who lack broad public support.
We saw this dynamic play out during the 2021 gubernatorial recall attempt.
Although voters overwhelmingly rejected the recall by nearly the exact margin as the original gubernatorial election, California taxpayers were forced to pay over **$200 million** for an unnecessary election.
Nearly 70% of California likely voters called the effort a waste of taxpayer money.
Had the recall succeeded, the leading replacement candidate would have taken office with only about 28% support from recall voters.
Proposition 5 enacts a single, commonsense fix to restore fairness and integrity: **it removes the second question from state recall ballots.**

## Should successor elections be eliminated from recall elections of state officials?
When a state legislator or a statewide official such as the governor faces a recall, voters are asked two questions: Should the lawmaker or official be removed from office?
And who should replace them?
Proposition 5 would eliminate the successor question.
If a statewide officeholder is recalled, the governor would appoint a replacement, while legislative vacancies would be filled by special election.
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would serve until another governor is elected.
## Yes Argument
California’s current recall system allows a replacement candidate to take office without winning the support of a majority of voters.
In the unsuccessful 2021 recall of Gov.
Gavin Newsom, the top replacement candidate received the support of just 28% of voters in the recall election — with millions of voters simply leaving the second question blank.
Getting rid of the replacement question keeps the recall election focused on the official facing removal.

Proposition 5 takes away the ability of Californians to choose their leaders.
Voters who recall a governor, attorney general or secretary of state should not have to wait months to pick a replacement — all while the position is filled by someone who was not elected to the job.
California’s recall system has worked well for more than a century and doesn’t need to be changed.

Constitutional Amendment
Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers
Amends the California Constitution to remove the choice of a successor from recall elections. Allows vacancies created by recalls to be filled under succession rules for state officers.
SPUR's Recommendation
Prop. 5 would help California avoid scenarios in which a successor can take statewide office with only a small plurality of votes. It would eliminate an incentive structure that has made recalls an attractive strategic partisan tool for removing elected officials without majority support. Replacing a plurality-rule special election with an institutional process tied to officials who themselves were elected by a majority of voters represents a more democratic and coherent outcome than the status quo.
Vote YES
What Prop. 5 Would Do
Proposition 5 would amend the California Constitution to change how state officer recall elections work in three key ways. 1
First, when voters choose to recall an elected official, they also choose that person’s successor on the same ballot. Prop. 5 would eliminate the successor election and instead fill the office through existing constitutional succession rules. These rules require the governor to fill non-legislative office vacancies (e.g., secretary of state, attorney general, controller) by appointment, and special elections to fill legislative office vacancies (senator, assemblymember).
Second, if a governor is recalled, Prop. 5 would require the lieutenant governor to assume the governorship for the remainder of the term. If the governor is successfully recalled before the close of nomination for the next statewide election, a special election would be held at the next statewide primary. This special election would prevent an unelected appointed governor from holding office for a full four-year term. 2
Third, Prop. 5 removes the prohibition on recalled officers running for the same office in a subsequent special election to fill their seat.
State Senator Josh Newman, who was recalled in 2019, and Assemblymember Isaac Bryan introduced the measure in 2023. The legislation was referred to the 2026 state ballot and requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass.
The Backstory
California voters authorized the recall process in 1911 through a ballot measure that passed with 76.8% of the vote. 3 The current recall process for state officers requires that voters elect a successor on the same ballot. The recalled official is prohibited from appearing as a candidate on the successor ballot. If a recall is successful, the replacement candidate who receives the most votes takes office immediately. 4
Current voting requirements for candidates to win regular elections (with two final candidates) differ from those for candidates in recall elections (with multiple candidates). A candidate can prevail in a recall successor race with a plurality of votes (the most votes, even if it's not more than 50%) rather than a majority (more than 50%). All voters may vote for a replacement candidate on the same ballot as the recall, regardless of whether they voted yes or no on the initial recall question. In the successful 2003 gubernatorial recall, Governor Arnold Schwarzenegger replaced Governor Gray Davis with only 48.6% of the vote. The attempted 2021 recall of Governor Gavin Newsom renewed attention to the process.
Most states that allow recalls already use either established succession rules or a separate special election. Since 1913, 179 recall attempts have targeted California state elected officials; 11 qualified for the ballot, and six officials were ultimately recalled. 5
The current recall system benefits the minority party in state politics because it offers an additional opportunity outside the normal election cycle to elect minority-party candidates. This election would occur at a moment of discontent with the majority-party officeholder, which is likely to increase the minority party’s chances of electing its candidate. In the near term, this advantage would favor Republicans, given that Democrats have held a majority in both the state legislature and the governorship since 2011.
State Gubernatorial Recall Provisions
Source: Ballotpedia, States with gubernatorial recall provisions (https://ballotpedia.org/States_with_gubernatorial_recall_provisions) .
Equity Impacts
Prop. 5’s equity implications are largely procedural rather than direct, but two dynamics are worth weighing.
First, the current successor-election system allows a candidate to take statewide office with a plurality of the vote — sometimes well under 50% — which can dilute the influence of any single bloc of voters, including communities of color. The current dynamic of off-cycle election timing is known to widen underrepresentation by shrinking and skewing the electorate toward already-engaged, disproportionately white and older voters. 6 Prop. 5 would increase the likelihood that gubernatorial successor elections are pushed to an on-cycle election, reducing the risk of underrepresentation from various voting blocs.
Second, eliminating the simultaneous successor vote does reduce one direct opportunity for voters to weigh in on a successor, which could be read as narrowing immediate civic participation. However, the constitutional succession process (e.g., replacing a recalled governor with the lieutenant governor, who was elected statewide) preserves a democratically legitimate alternative.
Pros
Prop. 5 would reduce the risk that a recall election would install an officeholder who lacks majority support. The change would align recall outcomes more closely with how California fills other vacancies.
The measure would discourage political actors from using recalls as a strategic end-run around the normal election cycle by calculating they could win a low-turnout plurality race even without majority public support.
It would provide more predictability and stability in succession for gubernatorial recalls because the lieutenant governor (already elected statewide) fills the vacancy under established, non-ad-hoc rules rather than through a compressed, high-stakes special election.
It would clarify decisions for voters who may be confused by the current successor election process, which is inherently more complicated than a single choice to recall or not recall an officer.
It would reduce the likelihood that voters would choose not to recall an elected officer because they are concerned about their successor. It would increase the likelihood that votes are cast to address actual non-partisan concerns about the officer targeted by the recall election.
Cons
Prop. 5 would require an additional election for recalls in the legislature, which could increase the cost of filling a vacancy in those seats.
The measure would allow appointees who were not elected to hold the governorship and preside over a lame-duck period, thereby potentially weakening the leadership’s ability to enact strong policy.

Proposition 5: Statewide Officers
Proposition 5: Statewide Officers
Proposition 5: Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Recall Reform, Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment
Summary
The California Senate introduced Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (SCA) in January of 2023. As the Legislature cannot amend the California Constitution by passing legislation, the amendment must be approved by California voters. The Senate passed the bill in February of 2024 and the Assembly passed an amended version in August of 2024. The Senate agreed with the changes to the bill sending the proposed constitutional amendment to voters on the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 5.
Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process. Specifically, it would eliminate the part of the ballot that asks voters to choose a replacement for the official being recalled. If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law. Legislative vacancies would generally be filled through a separate special election, while most other statewide offices would be filled by appointment by the Governor. If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would take over, either temporarily until the next statewide election or for the remainder of the term, depending on when the recall occurs.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
The financial impact would depend on how often recalls occur and which offices are involved. Costs could increase by millions of dollars when a recall creates a vacancy that requires a separate special election, particularly for legislative offices. At the same time, eliminating replacement candidates from recall ballots could save millions in some elections by reducing ballot and election-material costs. Overall, Proposition 5 could result in either costs or savings of potentially millions of dollars per recall election, although the effect would be very small compared with the state’s overall budget.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote supports changing California’s recall process so voters would decide only whether to remove an official, with the vacancy filled later under state law. A recalled official could run again, and the Lieutenant Governor would generally replace a recalled Governor.
NO: A “no” vote supports keeping the current recall process, in which voters decide whether to remove an official and simultaneously vote on who should replace that official if the recall succeeds.

Pro Con
Supporters argue that the current recall system can allow a replacement candidate to win with only a small share of the vote, particularly in low-turnout elections. They claim that Proposition 5 would make recalls more democratic and less confusing for voters while reducing opportunities to use recalls for political manipulation.
Opponents argue that voters should have the right to choose a Governor’s replacement at the time when they approve a recall. They say automatically allowing the Lieutenant Governor to take over could leave voters with a leader who shares the recalled Governor’s political views, limiting voter choice and weakening the purpose of the recall process.

Democrats want to change the rules for recall elections. Voters get their say with Prop. 5
by
CalMatters (https://www.almanacnews.com/author/calmatters/)

This story was originally published by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/). Sign up (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/) for their newsletters.
Sacramento State political science professor Kim Nalder was working out at a Sacramento gym in 2003 when she overheard a conversation about the upcoming recall election of then-Gov. Gray Davis, a Democrat.
She remembers “guys in the weight room just saying, like, “How cool would that be to have Arnold Schwarzenegger as our governor?’” she said. “It had nothing to do with policy at all.”
A few months later, the international action film star triumphed in a field of 135 candidates to replace Davis, who’d been re-elected the year before but had come under fire for rolling blackouts in the state and unpopular vehicle license fees. “The Governator” went on to serve nearly two terms.
If the election were just about whether or not Davis should keep his job, and not also who should replace him if he were recalled, Nalder doubts the Republican Schwarzenegger would ever have taken office. Accompanying him on the ballot were a host of other colorful characters, including actor Gary Coleman and porn star Mary Carey. Per the rules of the recall, the candidate with the most votes, not necessarily the majority, wins.
“I just think the recall probably wouldn’t have happened — because there wasn’t that much upset at Davis himself — if we didn’t, you know, have any fun alternatives,” she said.
California voters this year are deciding whether to approve Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/), which would do away with “the second question” of who should replace a state elected official if they are recalled. Instead, depending on the office and the timing, a replacement would be appointed or elected in a special election.
The measure was placed on the November ballot by Democratic lawmakers in 2024 with the support of the secretary of state and good governance groups Common Cause and League of Women Voters. It came in response to the 2021 attempted recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing that it would dilute the power of the voters and add costs associated with follow-up special elections.
However, with 14 propositions on the ballot and not a dollar raised so far in support or opposition, both sides may have to rely on voters’ gut reactions.
The “weak gazelle”
Aside from the recall of Davis, the only other successful state recall this century was that of the author of Prop. 5, Democrat Josh Newman.
In 2017, Newman was a freshman lawmaker representing a purple Southern California district when he joined 27 of his colleagues in approving the gas tax (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article143237054.html), which added a 12 cent surcharge to every gallon of gas purchased in California to fund transportation projects. Republicans fiercely opposed the effort, arguing new taxes weren’t necessary. The bill passed with the bare minimum of votes.
Less than two weeks later, then-conservative commentator and now-San Diego Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014) told Orange County talk show hosts that gas tax opponents needed to use the “gazelle strategy,” to begin taking out lawmakers who’d approved the tax.
“We’ve identified that weak gazelle, the slowest gazelle, the one with the limp,” he said. “And that’s Josh Newman, in Orange County.”
Why Newman? Because he was elected by the slimmest margin of any senator, fewer than 2,500 votes.
In the ensuing weeks, DeMaio’s organization, Reform California, led the effort to recall Newman, helping to collect more than 64,000 signatures — equivalent to 20% of voters in the last election — and centering its campaign on Newman’s “deciding vote” on the tax.
Close to 60% of voters chose to recall Newman in June 2018, replacing him with Republican Ling Ling Chang. The recall ended the Democrats’ supermajority in the state Senate.
In a recent interview with CalMatters, DeMaio stood by his “weak gazelle” strategy.
“If voters want to stop something from happening and being repeated, then mid-term, sometimes the only thing they can do is to use a recall as a way of expressing their opposition,” he said.
But Newman said that kind of “political gamesmanship” was not what former progressive governor Hiram Johnson intended when he proposed the law in 1911.
In a speech (https://governors.library.ca.gov/addresses/23-hjohnson01.html#:~:text=the%20precautionary%20measure%20by%20which%20a%20recalcitrant%20official%20can%20be%20removed%20is%20designated%20the%20%E2%80%9CRecall.%E2%80%9D), Johnson characterized the recall process as “the precautionary measure by which a recalcitrant official can be removed.”
Newman said he doesn’t feel he fit that bill.
“I didn’t do anything other than cast a tough vote,” he said. “Was I malfeasant? I hardly think so. Especially given the state of the state’s road systems at the time.”
Newman made recall reform one of his priorities when he was elected back into office in 2020. After an expensive recall election (https://calmatters.org/gavin-newsom-recall-election/) for Newsom, other Democrats had the political will and Newman put forward Senate Constitutional Amendment 1, which became Prop. 5.
Newman said the title of the proposition, which says that it “Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers,” may confuse voters, since legislators do not hold statewide office, though all California legislative races would be affected by the change.
How would it work?
If Prop. 5 passes, eliminating the replacement question, the governor would call a special election within about four months to replace a recalled state senator or assemblymember. If the governor was recalled within the first two years of their term, the secretary of state would call a special election. If they are in the second two years of their term, the lieutenant governor would finish the governor’s term. The ousted official would be allowed to run for the same office in the special election.
If a statewide official such as the state treasurer, attorney general, or insurance commissioner were recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement to serve until the next scheduled election.
If Prop. 5 were to pass, DeMaio said the gap in representation may dissuade voters from approving a recall, even if they want a change.
“The argument will now be made, if Prop. 5 passes, that if you vote yes on recall, then you’re going to be without a representative for months, if not longer, and so you’re going to silence your community,” he said.
He said extra special elections would lead to higher costs to taxpayers. The 2021 attempted recall of Newsom cost about $200 million to administer — a cost that would double if there were two separate elections.
However, Nalder suspects the change would lead to fewer recalls in general, likely a guiding force in Democrats’ support of the effort.
“It’s relatively easy to get the signatures, and it causes a lot of chaos and costs a lot of extra money,” she said. “That’s easier for Democrats to want to change because they’re the ones who win more in the races.”
A Public Policy Institute of California poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found the measure faces long odds, though: 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote “no” and just 35% said they would vote “yes.”
Nalder said the poll was conducted before voters had done their ballot homework, and upon learning more, they’ll likely align with their party’s positions.

Endorsement: Prop 5 has a flaw so bizarre even its author doesn’t like it
Proposition 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 8, 2026
So much has happened in American politics since 2021 that the recall election of California Gov. Gavin Newsom, which he overwhelmingly defeated, feels like a distant memory.
Proposition 5 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot puts recalls back in the spotlight.

Authored by (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1) former Democratic state Sen. Josh Newman of Fullerton — who was recalled in 2018, won reelection in 2020 and lost again in 2024 — Prop 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.

Here’s how the current process works:
To recall a statewide official, proponents must gather signatures totaling at least 12% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the prior election. For the Newsom recall, that threshold was 1.3 million signatures (https://admin.cdn.sos.ca.gov/elections/ccrov/2025/march/25024ra.pdf). To recall members of the state Assembly and Senate, the minimum number of signatures is 20% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the last election — for Newman’s recall, that threshold was about 63,600 signatures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/news-releases-and-advisories/2018-news-releases-and-advisories/recall-signatures-senate-district-29-certified).
Once a recall qualifies, voters then receive a ballot with two questions — one, should this official be recalled, and two, who should replace them? — and a list of replacement candidates. If a simple majority votes in favor of the recall, the replacement candidate who receives the most votes wins — even if that candidate only gets a fraction of the votes against the recall.
The two-question setup is confusing — only six other states use it (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials). And permitting someone to be elected without majority support is undemocratic. Furthermore, given the distraction and price of recalls — Newsom’s cost about $200 million during (https://apnews.com/article/elections-california-legislature-gavin-newsom-state-legislature-f8b78745cc5376dc4836d914352f2116) the most fraught moments of the pandemic — they should be reserved for cases of serious misconduct or abject unfitness, not petty grievances.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Even though only 11 recalls of state-level officials have qualified for the ballot since 1913, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), California could benefit from raising the bar. Its signature-gathering threshold is among the lowest in the nation (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/Report266.pdf).
But Prop 5 doesn’t grapple with this issue.
Instead, it would eliminate the second question from the recall ballot, meaning voters would decide only whether the official should be removed.
If a majority says yes, one of three things would happen:
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would automatically step into the role. If the recall happens in the first half of a governor’s four-year term before the nomination period ends for the next statewide election, the lieutenant governor would serve until that election takes place and voters choose the next governor. But if the recall happens after that point, the lieutenant governor would finish the rest of the governor’s term.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
If another statewide official — such as the lieutenant governor, attorney general or secretary of state — is recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement. The governor already follows this process for statewide officials who die, resign or accept a different job.
And if a member of the state Legislature is recalled, the governor would call a special election for their replacement — mirroring the existing process for a lawmaker who dies, resigns or takes a different job. As the Legislative Analyst’s office notes (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), if this special election couldn’t be consolidated with an already scheduled election, it could cost state and local election officials “millions of dollars” to administer.
Newman argued to us that eliminating the second question reduces “partisan games” and prevents candidates with minority support from winning elections.
We agree that the second question is problematic and we might support its removal in isolation. But Prop 5 contains a completely unnecessary provision that permits recalled officials to run in the very special election designed to replace them — overturning a ban in the California Constitution (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-15/).
This is particularly egregious because incumbents fighting recall attempts can generally raise unlimited funds from donors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=85315.&lawCode=GOV). Although state law prohibits that money from being used for other campaigns, a recalled official in a special election is unlikely to forget whatever limitless support they received from wealthy special interests.

Newman himself couldn’t explain why Prop 5 contains that provision.
“I’m honestly not sure,” he said. “It wouldn’t pain me if it wasn’t there.”

But it is there. And the inability or unwillingness of lawmakers to put forth a simple, clean reform effort is reason enough for voters to reject this measure.
California’s recall process can certainly be improved, but the problem isn’t so dire that voters need to accept Prop 5’s glaring flaw.

Opponents argue this initiative strips power from citizens and hands it directly to Sacramento political insiders

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 4:32 PM PST | UPDATED: November 2, 2026 at 6:07 PM PST
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 5, which changes the recall process for statewide elected officials. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=5&year=2026), the measure would remove from the question of who should replace the recalled official and proposes a special election to determine the replacement. In the meantime, the governor would choose who would fill the vacancy. In the case of a governor’s recall, the lieutenant governor would fill the vacancy until the next election.
Voting “yes” means the governor plays a much bigger role in replacing recalled officials and the lieutenant governor is a recall away from taking power (until the next election).
Voting “no” means the voters continue to choose replacements for recalled officials.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment, say this will simplify the recall process so we don’t end up with an overwhelming number of candidates on the ballot in a recall. With a greater number of candidates on the ballot, a candidate could win the election without a majority.
Opponents are uncomfortable with the increase in power given to the governor and insist it’s the people’s right to choose a governor’s replacement. They also say the lieutenant governor, with their proximity to the governor, would not represent the big change the people would have requested by voting for a recall.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/).
What problem would Prop. 5 create?
A disincentive for the people to self-govern, leading to more distrust of government and restlessness of the “masses.” After a time of withdrawal and lack of participation, the people will feel and react to their oppression in a negative way. Oppressed people eventually revolt, and it’s never pretty.

We asked the Yes on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
Currently, the recall process allows a candidate to win office without a majority. Why is that a system not worth reforming?
Under the current system, the democratic process of self-governance is served, and infinite amounts of taxpayer funds are saved by the current one-step process.
Prop. 5 “reforms” the current process by taking power from the people, and — worse — punishing the people for having the audacity to self-govern.
In the case of a recall, the term of office is limited to the remainder of the term of the recalled individual, and awarding the win to the person receiving a plurality in a crowded field is much more protective of the “democratic process” than adopting the changes proposed by Prop. 5, where the Sacramento insiders are the winners, hundreds of millions of dollars are wasted, and democracy dies.
If this measure isn’t a solution for fixing the recall process, do you have an alternate proposal?
This question pre-supposes the recall process needs fixing. The current process, wherein a recall decision and a filling of the recalled position in the case of recall success on the same ballot is efficient, fiscally responsible and respectful to the public.
The suggestion that the cost of having part two of the recall ballot is negligible, let alone millions of dollars, is patently absurd. Also absurd is the Prop. 5 proposal to eventually fill the recalled position with another, delayed election. The cost of a second election, which is likely to lead to a runoff costing more millions, is unarguable. That’s the very definition of absurd.
To quote Sen. Jones, “Our recall process is only ‘broke’ for those who find themselves on the business end of it, like Proposition 5’s author did when he (voted to raise) taxes after breaking campaign promises.”
What’s the biggest misconception about Prop. 5?
That there’s something wrong with the current system, and that CA legislators have any respect for a government of, by and for the people. CA is no longer a republic, but a socialist oligarchy. The power of the people to govern themselves has been so diminished already as to be virtually eliminated, and Prop. 5 is another step to seal the deal for complete power of the elite.
What did we miss? What didn’t we ask that our readers should know?
The element of Prop. 5 dealing with gubernatorial succession is also faulty. Yes, the people ostensibly elected a lieutenant governor, to serve as governor in the event of incapacity or death of the elected governor, not in the event of the governor’s disgrace — by which the lieutenant governor is surely tainted.
If the lieutenant governor wishes to succeed the governor in the event of a recall, that person may appear on the second portion of the ballot.
Chances are virtually 100% that if the people have grown disenchanted with the governor’s performance, they will be equally unwilling to be represented in that office by the second in command — almost certainly complicit in every act of disappointment and betrayal by the governor.

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 5, which changes the recall process for statewide elected officials. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=5&year=2026), the measure would remove from the question of who should replace the recalled official and proposes a special election to determine the replacement. In the meantime, the governor would choose who would fill the vacancy. In the case of a governor’s recall, the lieutenant governor would fill the vacancy until the next election.
Voting “yes” means the governor plays a much bigger role in replacing recalled officials and the lieutenant governor is a recall away from taking power (until the next election).
Voting “no” means the voters continue to choose replacements for recalled officials.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment, say this will simplify the recall process so we don’t end up with an overwhelming number of candidates on the ballot in a recall. With a greater number of candidates on the ballot, a candidate could win the election without a majority.
Opponents are uncomfortable with the increase in power given to the governor and insist it’s the people’s right to choose a governor’s replacement. They also say the lieutenant governor, with their proximity to the governor, would not represent the big change the people would have requested by voting for a recall.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem does Prop. 5 solve?
In its current form, a state-level recall ballot asks two questions in sequence: first, whether to remove an elected official, and second, who should immediately replace them. Although removal requires a majority vote, replacement doesn’t; whoever gets the most votes takes office, even if it’s by a small plurality in a crowded field. That mismatch can mean that an officeholder ousted by majority vote can be replaced by someone with far less support, and it gives well-organized interest groups a powerful incentive to instigate a recall in order to install a preferred candidate who wouldn’t have majority support under normal conditions. Prop. 5 fixes that mismatch by removing the replacement question and filling a vacancy under existing succession law instead.

Why is this the best solution?
Prop. 5 is the best solution because it fixes the specific, politically exploitable flaw — the plurality replacement provision — while still maintaining the recall as a powerful tool of direct democracy. Under its provisions, if a governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor, already duly elected by a majority of Californians statewide, steps in. If a recall takes place in the first two years of the term and before the filing deadline for the next statewide election, voters would still get a special election for a permanent successor, with a runoff if needed to achieve a majority. If the recall takes place later in the term, the lieutenant governor would serve out the remainder of an ousted governor’s term, the same as if they were to leave office for some other reason. In the event of a recall of other state-level officers, those offices would be filled under existing vacancy replacement provisions.
Why would Californians want to remove someone from office but forfeit to the governor their current right to immediately choose a successor?
Two corrections worth making: In the event of a gubernatorial recall, it wouldn’t be the governor who gains power but the lieutenant governor, a separately elected constitutional officer who is, by virtue of California’s Constitution, explicitly and deliberately next in the line of succession. Intrinsic to any lieutenant governor’s campaign is the assertion that he or she is most qualified to step in if events so demand. Second, voters aren’t forfeiting a choice: If a governor is recalled early in their term, Californians would still elect a permanent successor by majority through a special election. This is a sensible change from the current format, where, in the event of a gubernatorial recall, a replacement candidate can become governor of the largest and most important state in the country with only a small plurality, in a special election decided by a reduced electorate in a low-information and highly politicized environment.
Explain how this empowers majority rule and why that matters.
As it currently stands, while recalling a state-level elected official requires majority support, replacing them doesn’t. Only a plurality is required, which could be as low as 20% in a crowded replacement field. Prop. 5 closes that gap. When a successor election is held, if no one wins a majority outright, it would go to a runoff. So, whoever ultimately holds the office would have secured the support of more than half the voters, not just the largest slice of a fractured field. This is the standard California already applies to nearly every other office and election scenario. A recall shouldn’t be the one process where a candidate can take power without the validation of majority voter support.
How does this measure stop political groups from abusing the recall process?
It removes the existing incentive for political gamesmanship at the expense of electoral integrity. As it stands, a well-funded, motivated minority can force a recall and realistically expect its preferred candidate to win the replacement seat with a small plurality, sometimes far fewer votes than the officeholder who was removed. That’s a low bar for a high-value prize, and it’s why some recalls have been criticized as backdoor attempts to grab a seat that couldn’t be won in a regular election. Prop. 5 raises the bar and removes that incentive: Voters will still be able to remove a corrupt or malfeasant official, but it removes the strategic upside of gaming a plurality-only replacement. Instead, a replacement would be made in the normal order, and in the next election, the winner would ultimately secure a majority, with a runoff if needed.
How would this save taxpayers money?
First and foremost, by changing the incentive structure by eliminating the second question, Prop. 5 would save taxpayers money by reducing the likelihood of hyperpartisan recalls like the one which targeted Gov. Newson in 2021, which cost California taxpayers more than $200 million dollars in the midst of an unprecedented public health emergency where those funds were desperately needed for other purposes. California voters to decide on Prop 5 changes to recall election process | California Politics 360
Updated: 8:25 AM PDT Jul 19, 2026
Editorial Standards ⓘ (https://www.kcra.com/article/hearst-television-news-policy-statements/14471973)
Edie Lambert (https://www.kcra.com/news-team/b03bf5f3-3097-4d57-9469-1333f2abd98a)
Anchor/Reporter (https://www.kcra.com/news-team/b03bf5f3-3097-4d57-9469-1333f2abd98a)
Voters are being asked whether they want to change the rules for recalling California state leaders.
Proposition 5 would limit recall ballots to just one yes-or-no question: Should an elected official be recalled from office?
Advertisement
Currently, recall ballots also have a second section where voters are asked to choose a successor if the recall passes. Prop 5 would eliminate that second section. If the recall passes, a new leader is chosen later in a separate process.
Former State Senator Josh Newman wrote Prop 5, arguing that while the recall tool was originally intended to allow voters to remove unfit or corrupt officials, it's become a political weapon to try to seize power.
"The presence of that second question in today's politics creates a set of incentives that makes it more likely that we'll have recalls that have nothing to do with integrity, and more to do with politics," he explained.
Newman knows a lot about recalls. While representing an Orange County district, the Democratic State Senator angered some constituents after voting to raise the state's gas tax. He was recalled in a 2018 election by a 58% vote. But he points out that he still had 42% of voters supporting him, and he was replaced in the same election by Republican Ling Ling Chang, who only had 34% of the vote.
"Not only is that not a majority, but the proof that that is not sustainable, is that I then got re-elected in 2020 with a clear majority," said Newman.
Constitutional law experts, including the Dean of the University of California, Berkeley School of Law, Erwin Chemerinsky, have argued California's recall process violates the principle of "one person, one vote", where every voter has equal influence. They say the current recall process is flawed because the first section, the yes-or-no question that decides the recall, is a majority vote. However, in the second section, if the recall passes the candidate with the most votes wins. They don't need a majority. The target of a recall can receive more votes than any other candidate on the ballot, but still be removed from office.
"It's the smash and grab equivalent in politics," said Newman. "You create enough chaos, and there's an issue and you evict an elected official. Now, if they're corrupt, that's one thing. But to replace them with somebody who lacks majority support runs counter to what most people expect out of elections."
Critics of Prop 5 say it's not the solution.
"It's very punitive. And it's just simply the state saying, we don't want you to self-govern, forget it," explained Ruth Weiss, Director of Legislative Oversight for Election Integrity Project California. In particular, she questions the way recalled officials would be replaced.
Under Prop 5, recalls are treated as a standard vacancy with succession rules spelled out in the State Constitution. If a Governor is ousted, depending on the timing, either the lieutenant governor takes over for the remainder of the term or there's a special election. For the other statewide offices, the governor appoints a successor until the next regularly scheduled election. Recalled members of the state legislature are replaced in special elections.
"Stepping into the position would be someone that people did not choose, when it is so easy and not any more expensive at all to allow the people to choose the replacement of the person they're recalling on the same exact ballot," said Weiss. "There's no legitimate reason not to keep the recall the way it has been."
Prop 5 prevents a recalled official from being appointed to the same job, but they could run in the next election where it would take a majority vote to get their job back.
Critics also question what Prop 5 would cost, and there's no direct answer. Specials elections can be expensive. The 2021 recall election targeting Governor Gavin Newsom cost taxpayers $276 million. However, some special elections can be consolidated with a regularly- scheduled election, which is much cheaper. Proponents of Prop 5 say if it results in fewer recalls, it would save money.
Voters will decide Prop 5 in California's General Election on November 3, 2026.

California Proposition 5 would change state recall elections. Here's what to know.
By
Darrielle Fair
October 12, 2026 / 6:06 PM PDT
/ CBS Sacramento
Add CBS News on Google (https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=cbsnews.com)
California voters will decide in November whether to overhaul the state's recall election process.
Proposition 5, authored by former Democratic state Sen. Josh Newman, would change how California fills vacancies when state officials are recalled. Under the current system, voters decide whether to remove an official and simultaneously select a potential replacement.
If approved, Proposition 5 would separate those decisions, with vacancies generally filled through subsequent special elections or appointments, depending on the office. The measure also includes specific rules for replacing a governor and would allow a recalled official to run in a special election to fill the position.
A September poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) from the Public Policy Institute of California found that 59% of likely voters said they would vote against Proposition 5, while 35% said they would vote in favor. Another 5% were undecided.
The measure will appear on California's Nov. 3, 2026, general election ballot.
The proposal comes after California's failed 2021 effort to recall Gov. Gavin Newsom, which cost taxpayers more than $200 million, according to Newman.
But the measure faces opposition from Republicans who argue the existing system works and that changing it would limit voters' ability to choose their leaders.
Why Proposition 5 was introduced
California's recall process dates back more than a century. While recall efforts against state officials have been relatively rare, the 2003 recall of Democratic Gov. Gray Davis resulted in Republican Arnold Schwarzenegger taking office after winning a crowded replacement contest.
In 2018, Newman, a Democrat representing Orange County, became the target of a recall campaign. Nearly 60% of voters supported removing him from office, and his Republican opponent, Ling Ling Chang, replaced him.
Newman later won his seat back in the 2020 election. He said the experience helped shape his push to reform the recall system.
"My replacement was actually the same person whom I had defeated in the '26 election, 2016 election. And then I succeeded in getting reelected in 2020 by a fairly persuasive margin. And I think the point here is she actually took office with only 31% of the vote."
Newman argues the current system can allow a replacement candidate to take office without winning majority support, even when the official being recalled retains the support of most voters.
He said the failed Newsom recall also demonstrated the financial cost of the process.
"He won decisively, which is to say, the no vote beat the yes vote decisively by about the same margin as his original election and by his reelection. But at the end of the day, it wound up costing California taxpayers well over $200 million."
What would Proposition 5 change?
Under current law, voters in a recall election answer two questions: whether an elected official should be removed and who should replace that official if the recall succeeds.
Proposition 5 would eliminate the replacement question from the recall ballot.
The process for filling the vacancy would depend on the office. For legislative seats, a separate special election generally would be held. For other statewide offices, the governor would appoint a replacement under existing vacancy procedures.
The measure also establishes specific rules for the governor's office, including circumstances in which the lieutenant governor would serve as governor for the remainder of the term or until a successor is elected.
Supporters say the change would reduce political maneuvering and prevent candidates from taking office with only a small share of the vote.
Republicans oppose changing the recall process
Republican state Sen. Brian Jones argues California's existing recall system does not need to be changed.
"The recall process in California has been in place for over 100 years. It works. It's not used very often, so there's no reason to reform it at this point in time."
Jones also said elected officials should be accountable for their actions.
"Don't do something to get you recalled in the first place. If you make a promise to the voters, don't break the promise and you won't get recalled," he said.

A Democratic proposal would make recalls less appealing to the GOP

Leading Off
CA Ballot
California voters will decide this fall (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316600442.html) whether to overhaul the state’s rules for recall elections—rules that helped end one governor’s career while potentially saving another’s.
In any recall election against state-level officials, including the governor and members of the legislature, ballots currently consist of two separate questions (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) .
Voters are first asked a “yes” or “no” question about whether they want to remove the incumbent. They’re then asked to pick among the candidates vying to replace them—a contest that the incumbent cannot run in. These results, though, only matter if a majority votes “yes” on the first question.
If “yes” prevails, however, the successor could get elected with much less than a majority of the vote. That’s because all the candidates from all parties run on a single ballot without any primary or runoff to winnow the field.
But Proposition 5, which the state’s Democratic-led legislature voted to place on this year’s ballot back in 2024 (https://news.ballotpedia.org/2024/09/03/california-voters-will-decide-on-amendment-to-eliminate-successor-election-at-state-officer-recall-elections-in-2026/) , would amend the state constitution to change this process.
Under the proposed amendment, voters would simply be asked (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/news-releases-and-advisories/2026-news-releases-and-advisories/secretary-state-shirley-n-weber-phd-assigns-numbers-november-ballot-measures-invites-ballot-arguments) whether or not they want to recall the incumbent. If the governor is ousted, the lieutenant governor would automatically take over. Other offices, according to the proposed amendment (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/sca-1-24.pdf#page=3) , would be “filled in accordance with this Constitution and statute.”
If the governor is removed, what happens next would depend on the political calendar.
If the removal were to happen during the first two years of a governor’s term and ahead of the filing deadline for the next statewide primary, an election for their permanent replacement would take place alongside that primary.
All candidates would compete on a single ballot as they do now, but under the new rules, a majority would be necessary to win outright. If no one were to clear that threshold, the top-two vote-getters, regardless of party, would advance to a runoff coinciding with the November general election. In addition, the ousted governor would be eligible to compete in this contest.
If a recall were to take place outside this period, though, the lieutenant governor would serve as governor for the remainder of the term.
Two governors, both Democrats, have faced recall elections during the 21st century, but their fates diverged.
In 2003, Republicans targeted Gov. Gray Davis, who had won a second term the previous year, as the state’s ongoing energy crisis (https://www.cnn.com/2003/ALLPOLITICS/10/06/energy.crisis/index.html) left him unpopular. GOP Rep. Darrell Issa, one of the wealthiest members of Congress, bankrolled the recall campaign (https://www.the-downballot.com/p/morning-digest-after-saying-hes-not) with the intention of running to replace the incumbent.
A far-better known Republican, though, took advantage of Issa’s efforts. Arnold Schwarzenegger, the “Terminator” star who had spent decades at the top of Hollywood’s A-list, announced his campaign (https://www.cnn.com/2003/ALLPOLITICS/08/06/candidates.announce/) on “The Tonight Show” and instantly gobbled up all the attention. Issa, who no longer saw a path to victory, tearfully announced (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=T2tdOqCwqww) he would stay out of the race.
The GOP, though, wasn’t Davis’ only problem. Lt. Gov. Cruz Bustamante, a fellow Democrat, initially said (https://www.kqed.org/news/11870960/should-a-democrat-run-in-the-newsom-recall-we-asked-cruz-bustamante) he would “absolutely, 100%” not run as a replacement candidate, but he soon went back on that pledge and became one of the 135 people who placed their name on the ballot (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_California_gubernatorial_recall_election#/media/File:Sample_ballot_for_CA_recall.png) .
The lieutenant governor and his allies tried to thread the needle by pushing the slogan “No on recall, Yes on Bustamante.” However, they struggled to sell that awkward pitch even before Bustamante started criticizing the incumbent (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-sep-02-me-analysis2-story.html) in the evident hope that the recall would succeed and Bustamante would become his successor.
A 55-45 majority (https://uselectionatlas.org/RESULTS/state.php?fips=6&year=2003&f=0&off=5&elect=0) voted to remove Davis from office, but Californians didn’t want Bustamante as their new governor. Schwarzenegger instead prevailed over the massive field with 49% of the vote as Bustamante finished a distant second with 31%.
Gov. Gavin Newsom and his allies were determined to avoid a repeat of that debacle 18 years later when Republicans, who used the governor’s attendance at a high-end party (https://www.politico.com/states/california/story/2020/11/13/newsom-faces-backlash-after-attending-french-laundry-dinner-party-1336419) during the COVID pandemic as a pretext, placed a recall on the 2021 ballot.
Newsom’s side successfully discouraged (https://www.dailykos.com/stories/2021/3/1/2018561/elections/Morning-Digest-Top-New-York-Democrats-start-calling-for-Cuomo-to-be-primaried-but-who-will-run/#6) prominent Democrats from running as backup candidates and framed the race as a choice between the governor and far-right extremists.
Newsom’s argument became even easier when conservative radio host Larry Elder blew past (https://www.dailykos.com/stories/2021/9/15/2052274/elections/Morning-Digest-California-Gov-Gavin-Newsom-defeats-recall-vote-in-a-landslide/) more mainstream Republicans like former San Diego Mayor Kevin Faulconer when pollsters asked voters whom they favored on the second question.
Elder ultimately scored 48% (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/complete-sov.pdf#page=13) of the vote, while a little-known Democrat took a distant second with just 10%. But unlike in Schwarzenegger’s contest, the question proved to be meaningless. Voters rejected the recall 62-38, and Newsom went on to handily secure a second term the following year.
